source.title: Scaling Law for Language Models Training Considering Batch Size
source.authors: Xian Shuai; Yiding Wang; Yimeng Wu; Xin Jiang; Xiaozhe Ren

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains language models across parameter and data scales, measures loss, fits scaling laws, and evaluates extrapolations. It uses the same broad experimental approach as the original scaling-law studies, while adding batch size and learning rate.
record.gate_note: The paper reports equations for fitted loss and compute-optimal allocations, and qualitative loss comparisons for larger runs. It also reports downstream task scores. Some loss outcomes are only shown in figures, with the text describing their ordering. The comparison values cited from other studies are not recorded as results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study trains GPT-series models from 125M to 2.6B parameters on up to 300B tokens. It fits loss against N, D and C, and fits compute-optimal N and D, as the originals did (Sec. 4.1, Eq. 13–15). It then trains a compute-optimal 4.49B configuration against three 6.80B configurations at equal FLOPs (Sec. 4.5). Batch-size and learning-rate laws are the paper's main addition and fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that their 125M–2.6B runs establish a basic N–D compute-optimal law. They also derive batch-size power laws for fixed compute (in C) and fixed data (in D), and find that the optimal learning rate grows sub-linearly with batch size. Extrapolation runs at 4.49B and 6.80B 'validate our predicted laws'. The limitations they list are: frontier-point selection, a single fitting method, constant batch size, learning-rate scaling factors instead of schedules, unconsidered hyperparameters such as AdamW β2, and no models above 7B. Validation means ordering of configurations, not numeric loss prediction.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains GPT-series models and fits loss scaling in parameters, data, and compute, as in the original scaling-law approach, but adds batch-size and learning-rate sweeps. It uses its own data, infrastructure, and fitting procedure rather than explicitly replicating either original study.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that different frontier points can yield different envelopes and that initial regression guesses affect final fits, although multiple high-R-squared initializations produce similar results. Batch-size outcomes also vary with learning-rate scheme and available training tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch-size laws: Bopt is about 6.42e3·C^0.102 on the frontier and about 3.24e3·D^0.264 at fixed data. At equal N and D, a 3M batch beats a 0.25M batch downstream.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal global batch size grows as a power of compute on the frontier, and sub-linearly with data at fixed N and D.

fits_no_version.finding: For a 350M model, the optimal learning rate grows as B^γ with γ between 0.75 and 1, then plateaus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal learning rate grows sub-linearly with batch size up to a ceiling.

record.problems: The primary loss curves and extrapolation losses are presented as plots without numerical loss values in the text. The study does not state that the fitted losses are held-out. The basic scaling fits use models from 125M to 2.6B, and the authors note that frontier-point selection, fit initialization, training schedules, other hyperparameters, and larger-scale extrapolation may affect results. They do not test models larger than 7B.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise eligible reported findings were omitted.

untested.parts: Held-out loss is not reported; fits use training loss curves. N spans only 125M to 2.6B. There is no test of the power law when one factor is the bottleneck.

There is no quantitative extrapolation. No predicted loss is compared with observed loss for the 4.49B and 6.80B runs. Those runs use under 2x the compute of the largest fitted run, not orders of magnitude more. The 2.6B at 1T tokens (loss about 1.89) and 1B at 15T predictions are not checked.
Stability of the exponents across compute ranges or setups is not tested. The allocation is validated at only one compute budget (8.16e21).
Not tested. The 4.49B and 6.80B models differ only in hidden size, but they also differ in N and D, so this is not a shape test.
No downstream scaling curve across scale and no downstream prediction. The evidence is only the ordering of four equal-compute runs.
Parameter counting, schedules, data, and alternative fitting methods are not varied. The Discussion lists these as limitations without testing them.

missing.what: Overlaid runs with batch sizes from 1M to 32M under three learning-rate schemes, at 100B tokens, leave the FLOP-loss frontier unchanged. The frontier rests only on batch sizes of 0.5M or more. This bears on whether the compute-optimal split depends on setup.

The authors state they fit with only one method, unlike Hoffmann. They also derive L(N,D) under a constraint from Nopt and Dopt, which may accumulate error. This is a declared fitting choice, not a test.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 label is removed. The extrapolation compares configurations at one compute budget and reports no predicted loss values. That budget is under 2x the compute of the largest fitted run. The introduction says 4.3B/7B while the tables say 4.49B/6.80B, a minor inconsistency. The study's exponents (0.464/0.536) sit near Chinchilla and Llama-3 in Table 3, but those comparators are cited results, not this study's. The V6 evidence is weak: four equal-compute runs, loss given only in a figure, and ordering stated in text.

versions.untested_parts: The text does not state whether the fitted loss measurements are held-out or validation losses. It tests loss scaling over its reported model, token, and compute ranges, but does not separately establish every condition in which the other variables are not bottlenecks.
Extrapolations are reported for 4.49B and 6.80B models; the study does not test beyond 7B or with more training data.
The compute-optimal parameter and token trends are fitted on this study's setup and frontier; the study does not establish that the trend is universal across training setups.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns language-model pretraining and does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream scores are reported for four training configurations and five tasks plus an average; the study does not fit a general downstream-performance scaling curve across a broad range of scales.
The study discusses frontier selection and reports sensitivity to regression initialization, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, data, training schedules, or fitting methods.
